content: Rotifers are microscopic or nearly microscopic pseudocoelomate animals that belong to their own phylum. They were first described by John Harris in 1696, although Antonie van Leeuwenhoek is often mistakenly credited for this discovery. Harris also produced sketches of rotifers in 1703. These organisms are typically about 0.5 mm in length and are commonly found in freshwater environments worldwide, with a few species inhabiting saltwater. Rotifers exhibit various modes of locomotion: some are free-swimming and planktonic, others move by inching along substrates, and some are sessile, living within tubes or gelatinous structures. The name rotifer is derived from the Greek term meaning wheel-bearer, which refers to the corona, a structure composed of ciliated tufts around the mouth. When in motion, the corona resembles a spinning wheel. The cilia generate currents that direct food particles into the mouth, where they are processed by a specialized pharynx called the mastax. The mastax contains a calcified, jaw-like structure known as the trophi, which grinds the food. The cilia also aid in locomotion, propelling unattached rotifers through the water. Most free-living rotifers possess posterior toes that allow them to anchor themselves while feeding. Rotifers exhibit bilateral symmetry and come in a variety of shapes. Their body is covered by a well-developed cuticle, which can be either thick and rigid, giving the animal a box-like appearance, or flexible, resulting in a worm-like shape. These forms are referred to as loricate and illoricate, respectively. Like many other microscopic animals, adult rotifers often display eutely, meaning they have a fixed number of cells within a species, typically around 1,000. In the class Monogononta, males may be present or absent depending on the species and environmental conditions. In the absence of males, reproduction occurs via parthenogenesis, producing clonal offspring genetically identical to the parent. Some species produce two types of parthenogenetic eggs: one type develops into normal females, while the other, triggered by environmental changes, develops into degenerate males. These males lack a digestive system but possess a complete reproductive system, which they use to inseminate females, resulting in fertilized resting eggs. Resting eggs develop into zygotes capable of surviving extreme environmental conditions, such as winter or desiccation. When conditions improve, these eggs resume development and produce a new generation of females. The lifespan of monogonont females ranges from a few days to about three weeks. Bdelloid rotifers, in contrast, do not produce resting eggs but can survive prolonged periods of adverse conditions through desiccation. This ability, known as anhydrobiosis, allows them to contract into an inert form and lose nearly all body water during drought conditions. Upon rehydration, they resume activity within hours. Bdelloids can remain in this dry state for extended periods, with documented dormancy lasting up to nine years. Unlike other anhydrobiotic organisms, such as brine shrimp, which rely on the production of trehalose (a non-reducing disaccharide) for desiccation tolerance, bdelloids lack the ability to synthesize trehalose. Their genomes contain multiple divergent copies of each gene, suggesting a long history of asexual evolution. For example, four distinct copies of the hsp82 gene are found on different chromosomes, ruling out the possibility of homozygous sexual reproduction. There are approximately 2,000 species of rotifers, classified into three main classes: Monogononta, Bdelloidea, and Seisonidea. The parasitic group Acanthocephala is closely related to these classes. Together, these taxa are part of the superphylum Platyzoa. Monogononta is the largest group, comprising around 1,500 species. Bdelloidea is particularly notable for the absence of males and its ability to survive desiccation through cryptobiosis, becoming active again when environmental conditions improve. Rotifers inhabit a wide range of environments, including ponds, moist soil, and stagnant water. They can be free-swimming or sessile. Most rotifers are omnivorous, feeding on algae or decomposing organic material, although some species have been observed to exhibit cannibalistic behavior.
